terms.comment: What one lives on goes in the ablative: lacte atque pecore vīvunt (Caes. BG 4.1.8). Dum vīvō, as long as I live; ita vīvam!, as I live! (Cic. Fam. 2.13.3, Lewis & Short; Traupman 102).

evidence: Phaedr. 3.16.19: sīc vīva quod negārat tribuit mortua

phrases.latin: līberī quid agunt meī, quōs relīquī hīc, fīlium atque fīliam? — Vīvont, valent.
phrases.english: How are my children, whom I left here, my son and my daughter? — Alive and well.

phrases.latin: nēmō enim est tam senex quī sē annum nōn putet posse vīvere
phrases.english: for no one is so old that he does not think he can live another year

phrases.latin: neque multum frūmentō, sed maximam partem lacte atque pecore vīvunt
phrases.english: they live not much on grain, but mostly on milk and the meat of their herds

sources: Lewis & Short: vivo · Lewis & Short: vivus
